title: Science, technology and innovation: What kind of system does Nepal need? - The Annapurna Express
description: Science, technology and innovation: What kind of system does Nepal need?  The Annapurna Express
publisher.title: The Annapurna Express
full_article:
There is something encouraging about the Ministry responsible for Science, Technology and Innovation inviting the public to share ideas about Nepal’s science, technology and innovation (STI) system. It is a welcome step. A national STI system should not be designed only inside government offices. Researchers, universities, businesses, young people, local governments and citizens should all have a voice. But I think there is a bigger question here. How do we move from collecting ideas to actually building a system that can make something happen?

Social media can help open up public discussion. It allows people who may never write a policy paper or attend a government meeting to share their thoughts. But it also creates noise. A well researched recommendation, a personal opinion and an uninformed comment can appear side by side. Listening to people is important, but listening alone is not enough. We also need research evidence, institutional experience, expert knowledge and conversations with those who will eventually implement and use science and technology.

I write this as a Nepali researcher working in ICT and development, currently based in Norway. Norway is not a model that Nepal can simply copy. Our resources, institutions and circumstances are very different. But working here has made me think more deeply about a basic question: when a government invests public money in science and technology, what exactly are we trying to build?

For me, STI is not simply about producing research papers, developing new products or importing the latest technologies. It is about building a country's ability to understand its own problems, create knowledge, use technology, solve problems and learn from experience.

And perhaps this distinction matters more than we sometimes realize.

Take flash floods, for example. Nepal needs better ways of predicting floods, and technologies such as sensors, data analytics and artificial intelligence can certainly help. But a prediction alone does not save lives. Someone must collect and interpret the data, someone must make a reliable prediction, authorities must decide when to issue a warning, and that warning must reach communities in a form they understand and can act upon. If the technology works but the warning never reaches the people who need it, have we really solved anything?

This is one of the lessons from ICT for Development, or ICT4D. Technology does not work in isolation. It becomes useful through people, institutions, relationships and the conditions in which it is used. Perhaps this is also how we should think about Nepal’s STI system. Instead of asking only what technology we can develop, we should ask what problem we are trying to solve, who will use the solution, who benefits and what new capabilities it creates.

Nepal already has many of the pieces. We have universities, the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology (NAST), research institutions, government agencies, businesses, startups, local governments and communities. We also have Nepali scientists, engineers and professionals working abroad who could contribute in different ways. The problem is not necessarily the absence of knowledgeable people or institutions. It is that they often work separately.

An ecosystem does not mean that everyone does everything. It means that different actors have different roles and find ways to work toward shared goals. The Ministry should provide direction, create a supportive policy environment, connect institutions and ensure that public money is used responsibly. NAST has an important role in research, scientific advice and building research capacity. Universities develop knowledge and people. Businesses turn ideas into products and services. Government agencies understand sectoral challenges, while local governments and communities know how problems are experienced on the ground.

The challenge is to make these different strengths work together.

A useful starting point, therefore, is to ask what Nepal wants to become over the next 10 or 20 years. What are the national priorities? What knowledge, skills and technologies will be needed? What can we develop ourselves, what can we learn from others, and where would international collaboration make more sense than trying to do everything alone?

These questions also bring us to education. We cannot build a strong STI system without strong universities, researchers, laboratories and opportunities for young people. If climate science, agriculture, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, energy or disaster management are important national priorities, we need people who can work in these fields. Research capacity is not something that can be built through a short-term project or a funding announcement. It takes years of investment, institutional commitment and opportunities for people to develop their expertise.

We also need to recognize that not all research produces results in the same way or on the same timeline. Basic research in climate science, biodiversity, health or computing may take years before its benefits become visible. Applied research may address a more immediate problem, while prototypes and pilot projects test whether an idea works in practice. A technology deployed nationally must meet yet another set of expectations around cost, adoption, sustainability and public benefit.

We should not evaluate all these activities using the same criteria. Nor should we expect every research project to produce a commercial product. Sometimes research produces new knowledge, sometimes it develops people and institutions, and sometimes it shows us that an approach does not work. There is value in all three.

This brings me to something that I think deserves more attention: failure. Research involves uncertainty. A pilot project may not work as expected. An experiment may produce an unexpected result. A promising idea may turn out to be impractical. This is not necessarily wasted public money. The real waste is repeating the same mistakes without learning from them. Nepal needs a disciplined funding system that encourages good research, supports experimentation and evaluates results honestly. Strategic direction should come from the government, while funding decisions should be informed by independent scientific, technical, economic and social expertise.

And then there is artificial intelligence. It is difficult to have a conversation about science and technology today without mentioning AI. Nepal should certainly understand it, experiment with it and find meaningful ways to use it. But AI should not become the organizing principle of our STI policy. We should start with the problem, not the technology. In the case of floods, the question is how to reduce damage and protect communities. AI may be part of the answer, but it is unlikely to be the whole answer.

Ultimately, the success of Nepal’s STI system should not be measured only by the number of research papers, patents, startups, laboratories or prototypes it produces. These things matter, but they tell only part of the story. We should also ask whether our universities are becoming stronger research institutions, whether young researchers have opportunities, whether government agencies can use research in decision-making, whether Nepali businesses are developing the capacity to innovate, and whether local governments can access and use appropriate technologies.

Perhaps the most important question is not which technology Nepal should develop next, but what Nepal should be capable of doing 10 or 20 years from now that it cannot do today. That question changes the conversation. It moves us away from chasing technologies and toward building capabilities. It makes us think about research, education, institutions, infrastructure, international collaboration and public investment as connected parts of the same effort.

Nepal does not need to develop every new technology. We need to become better at understanding technology, producing knowledge, learning from others, adapting what we need and developing what matters to us. Our resources may be limited, but our ambition does not have to be. And perhaps that is where a national STI system should begin: not with a list of technologies we want to acquire, but with a clearer understanding of the kind of country we want to become.

title: India Approves Additional 615.02 MW Electricity Export from Nepal - Ratopati
description: India Approves Additional 615.02 MW Electricity Export from Nepal  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. On the eve of Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India, the Indian government has approved the export of an additional 615.02 megawatts of electricity from Nepal.

According to Nepal Electricity Authority spokesperson Achyut Ghimire, the approval for an additional 615.02 MW of electricity export was received today, as part of a gradual process of approvals for requests sent by the authority in June-July.

Spokesperson Ghimire stated that in addition to the 652 MW of electricity export already approved, an additional 615.02 MW has now been approved.

Via which medium and from which projects, how much export?

According to the information provided by spokesperson Ghimire, the total additional 615.02 MW of electricity for which approval has been received will be exported for sale in the Indian Energy Exchange Market through PTC and NVVN. Among these, 12 projects totaling 204.58 MW are through PTC.

Through PTC India, approval has been granted for the export of 204.58 MW of electricity from 12 hydropower projects via the 132 KV Bihar transmission line to the exchange market from November 18 to June 14, 2027.

PTC has also approved the export of 21.34 MW from Seti Hydropower. Through PTC, Seti Hydropower Project's 21.34 MW electricity has been approved for export to Bihar from November 18 to August 31, 2027. With this, a total of 225.92 MW of electricity for Bihar will be exported through PTC.

Ghimire informed that approval has been received for the export of 389.1 MW of electricity through NVVN via the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur 400 KV double circuit transmission line to the exchange market from November 18 to June 14, 2027.

The electricity will be exported to India through the Muzaffarpur-Dhalkebar 400 KV double circuit (DC), Kataiya-Kushaha 132 KV, Raxaul-Parwanipur 132 KV, and Ramnagar-Surajpura 132 KV cross-border transmission lines between Nepal and India.

Spokesperson Ghimire stated that approvals from the Indian side for the proposals sent by the authority earlier are still ongoing.

With the approval for the export of an additional 615.02 MW of electricity, Nepal is expected to earn significant revenue from electricity trade with India. In the last fiscal year, Nepal earned approximately 18 billion rupees (about 1.8 billion rupees) from net electricity exports to India.

title: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal - Explorersweb »
description: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:

An apparently unclimbed peak above 6,000m an aesthetic route manageable objective hazards an approach that was relatively accessible for a small team

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Not easy to reach

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Adventurous acclimatizing

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”

The Fang

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

Daara Peak on Google Earth.

The climb

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence

has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Exploration paradox

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

title: Media interaction highlights the role of journalists in raising awareness of AMR during WAAW 2026 - World Health Organization (WHO)
description: Media interaction highlights the role of journalists in raising awareness of AMR during WAAW 2026  World Health Organization (WHO)

full_article:
Lalitpur, Bagmati Province – Marking the start of World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW) 2026, WHO Country Office for Nepal, FAO Nepal, Global AMR Media Alliance (GAMA) Nepal and Health Journalists Forum Nepal jointly organized a media interaction programme to strengthen journalists’ understanding and reporting of AMR across human, animal and environmental health.

Held under the theme - “One Health, One Action: Prevent AMR Now”, the programme brought together more than 40 journalists, and representatives from the Ministry of Health and Food Safety (MoHFS) and the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment (MoAFE). Discussions highlighted the growing threat of AMR and its implications for human health, animal health, food safety and environment, underscoring the need for coordinated action across sectors.

JournalismPakistan.com | Published: 18 November 2026 | JP Asia Desk

The IFJ condemned the government's decision to forward the proposal without consulting media stakeholders. Summary

KATHMANDU — Journalists' organizations in Nepal have intensified opposition to proposed amendments to the Press Council Act, warning that the changes could expand regulatory oversight of online journalism and undermine press freedom.

The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) on November 18 condemned the government's decision to recommend the ordinance without consulting media stakeholders. The proposal was forwarded to President Ram Chandra Paudel following a Cabinet decision on November 3, but there has been no confirmed announcement that it has been promulgated.

Wider powers over online journalism

The proposed Press Council (First Amendment) Ordinance 2083 would broaden the definitions of media, journalism and journalists to include journalistic content published through social media and other digital platforms. Online news organizations and creators producing journalistic material would fall within the council's code of conduct and complaint procedures.

The amendments would also extend oversight to foreign journalists working for international news organizations and independent foreign journalists operating in Nepal. According to the IFJ, the council would gain the authority to initiate investigations without receiving a public complaint and monitor media organizations' social media activities.

Concerns over regulatory independence

The proposed expansion has raised concerns about the independence of media regulation. Although the Press Council is an autonomous body, its appointments are linked to the government, creating questions about how its additional powers might be exercised.

Nepali media reports have also identified provisions allowing the council to recommend the suspension of state facilities for repeated violations and prescribe how corrections must be published or broadcast. Critics fear that such measures could increase pressure on independent publishers, particularly smaller digital news organizations.

Journalists challenge ordinance

The Federation of Nepali Journalists (FNJ) has questioned the government's decision to pursue an ordinance while a separate Media Council Bill was being considered through the parliamentary process.

On November 6, a delegation led by FNJ President Nirmala Sharma met President Paudel and urged him not to issue the ordinance. The federation argued that bypassing parliamentary debate and consultation on legislation affecting journalism was inconsistent with democratic principles and constitutional protections for press freedom.

The FNJ also called for the withdrawal of the proposal and demanded that any amendments be developed through discussions with journalists, media organizations and other stakeholders.

Protest programme announced

Opposition has since developed into organized action. On November 17, the FNJ announced a phased protest programme addressing the ordinance, police actions against journalists and continuing violations of media workers' labour rights.

The federation scheduled a memorandum to the prime minister for November 18, followed by representations to parliamentary political parties on November 21, discussions with professional organizations and district-level gatherings on November 25. The announcement warned that further protests could follow if its demands were not addressed.

Police actions deepen concerns

The dispute comes against a backdrop of recent police actions involving journalists. On October 30, plainclothes officers reportedly entered media offices in Kathmandu without warrants and detained three journalists for questioning.

The IFJ identified them as Bishwamani Subedi of Nepal Press, Motive News editor Shobharaj Baral, and DNA Khabar editor Dhiraj Basnet. All three were subsequently released.

The FNJ has demanded an independent investigation into police entry into newsrooms and alleged mistreatment of journalists.

The IFJ said expanding the Press Council's authority without meaningful consultation threatened freedom of expression and urged the authorities to address journalists' concerns before proceeding.

The dispute now centres on whether Nepal's government will reconsider the proposed regulations or pursue changes despite opposition from journalist organizations. The president's decision on the ordinance remains a key unresolved question.

Online news outlets and creators producing journalistic content would fall under the council's code of conduct and complaint procedures.

The amendments would extend oversight to foreign journalists and allow the council to initiate investigations without a public complaint.

The IFJ condemned the move, criticizing the government for forwarding the ordinance without consulting media stakeholders.

Concerns were raised about regulatory independence, given the Press Council's appointments are linked to the government.

Key Questions & Answers What changes do the proposed amendments make? The amendments broaden definitions of media, journalism and journalists to include social media and digital platforms, extend oversight to foreign reporters, and allow the council to investigate without a public complaint. Why are journalists opposing the ordinance? Journalists and their organizations say the changes could expand regulatory control over online content, jeopardize press freedom and weaken the independence of media regulation. The International Federation of Journalists condemned the government's decision to forward the ordinance without consulting media stakeholders and warned of threats to media freedom. The proposal was forwarded to the president after a Cabinet decision; there has been no confirmed announcement of promulgation, and media groups continue to press for consultation and revision.

title: Nepal seeks global climate finance for $5bn recovery bill at COP31 - Everest Chronicle
description: Nepal seeks global climate finance for $5bn recovery bill at COP31  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
Nepal has urged the international community to provide faster and more accessible climate finance to vulnerable mountain nations, warning that it faces a recovery bill of $5 billion following a series of devastating disasters.

Addressing the 31st UN climate conference (COP31) in Antalya on Wednesday, Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to tackle the mounting threats facing mountain regions.

She said retreating snowlines, drying springs and increasingly erratic monsoon patterns were exposing Himalayan communities to a growing combination of droughts and devastating floods.

"I am here carrying the hopes of families who lost so much in the recent Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi disaster. They did nothing to cause this crisis, yet they paid the highest price," she told delegates.

The August disaster killed more than 1,400 people, left more than 5,000 missing and displaced thousands of families.

Chaudhary said mountain communities were bearing the consequences of climate change despite contributing little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving it.

"Mountains are the water towers of our planet. When they suffer, billions downstream feel the consequences," she said, arguing that the fate of mountain ecosystems was inseparable from global water security.

She outlined three priorities for the proposed mechanism: stronger scientific monitoring and early-warning systems, more accessible climate finance and greater fairness in international climate action.

On financing, she urged countries to make funding available before, during and after disasters, arguing that support must be rapid, simplified and largely grant-based.

She also proposed a dedicated rapid-response financing window under the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, saying existing arrangements were failing to deliver resources quickly enough to countries struck by climate-related disasters.

Making the case for climate justice, Chaudhary said Nepal accounted for less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, while forests covered nearly half its territory.

She cited the country's ranking as the world's 161st-largest emitter on a per-capita basis and its rapid adoption of electric vehicles as evidence of its efforts to pursue a lower-carbon development path.

"Yet we are now left with a recovery of $5 billion as we struggle to access the resources," she said. "This is not only a financing gap. It is a fairness gap."

The minister warned that damage to mountain ecosystems could be irreversible, rejecting the notion that temporarily exceeding global temperature targets would be without lasting consequences.

Chaudhary also pressed delegates to retain provisions on mountains in the draft COP31 cover decision, including a dedicated mountain work programme, a standing agenda item, a high-level political dialogue and an annual mountains dialogue.

The push comes after Nepal secured $20 million in funding from the UN's Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage following the August disaster. However, it failed to secure agreement at COP31 to make Himalayan climate impacts a separate formal agenda item, which would have given mountain issues a dedicated place in the conference's negotiations.

"This is not a favour to Nepal. It is a recognition long overdue," Chaudhary said, urging countries not to dilute the proposals.

She said families of victims from 34 countries affected by the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi disaster were watching the negotiations, alongside billions of people whose water supplies, food security and livelihoods depended on healthy mountain ecosystems.

"Let Antalya be remembered as the COP that finally listened to the mountains," she said.

publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 18: Preparations for the upcoming India visit of Prime Minister Balendra Shah have been intensified.

Prime Minister Shah is embarking on a two-day official visit to India on November 22 at the invitation of Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi.

Spokesperson of the Foreign Ministry, Lok Bahadur Poudel Chhetri, shared that the ministry has accelerated preparations for PM Shah's India visit.

"Internal preparations are being done regarding the details of the visit. The Ministry will make public it soon," mentioned Spokesperson Chhetri.

Emphasis would be laid on connectivity expansion between the two countries as well as discussion would be held in the matters of development assistance, tourism promotion and further strengthening people-to-people level relations during the visit.

It is also shared that agenda of air connectivity expansion, providing additional entry points to Nepal, railway and road network expansion, and infrastructure development of energy sector would be prioritized.

It has been expected that Janakpur-Adyodhya railway would be inaugurated as well as understanding would be reached to expand Jaynagar-Janakpur railway service up to Bardibas, possibility of Raxaul-Kathmandu railway during the visit.

Construction of roads and bridges, integrated check post and expansion of electricity transmission line are also the agenda of the discussion.

Similarly, issues of increasing support of India in post disaster reconstruction and in the areas of development construction would also be discussed.

The projects operated in Nepal with Indian assistance would be reviewed, completed projects would be inaugurated and handed over and discussion would be held to complete the under construction projects soon during the visit, it is learnt.

Likewise, it is also expected that the matter of launching some new development projects would also get priority as well as discussion would be held for tourism promotion between the two countries and further strengthening people-to-people relations during the visit.

Foreign Secretary of India, Vikram Misri, made a two-day official visit to Nepal on November 4 in course of preparation of India visit of Prime Minister Shah. (RSS)

title: Indian envoy meets Nepal PM Shah ahead of his visit to India - Daily Excelsior
description: Indian envoy meets Nepal PM Shah ahead of his visit to India  Daily Excelsior
publisher.title: Daily Excelsior
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nov 18: India's Ambassador Sudhakar Dalela on Wednesday called on Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah and discussed preparations for his proposed official visit to India.

According to the Prime Minister's Secretariat, Dalela informed Shah during their meeting at Singha Durbar that his upcoming bilateral talks with his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi will be historic and significant.

The development comes a day after Nepalese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chetri said the ministry is engaged in necessary preparations for Shah's forthcoming visit.

According to ministry sources, Shah will visit New Delhi on November 22. However, there has been no official announcement on the dates.

During the meeting, Dalela said that the visit's agenda was already finalised and that the relevant agencies had ramped up preparations to ensure its success.

The two sides also discussed ways to further strengthen the historical, cultural and geographical ties between India and Nepal.

Shah congratulated Dalela on his appointment as India's ambassador to Nepal and wished him a successful tenure.

He also thanked the Indian government for extending assistance to Nepal following the devastating Bhotekoshi flash floods in August that killed at least 1,500 people and left over 5,000 missing. (PTI)

title: Nepali Army has made key contribution in construction of road infrastructure: President Paudel - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepali Army has made key contribution in construction of road infrastructure: President Paudel  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Bagmati, Nov 18: President Ramchandra Paudel has said that the Nepali Army has been making significant contributions in terms of its constitutional duties and national security responsibilities as well as in the country's road infrastructure and development projects.

At the 'breakthrough' ceremony of the Mahadevtar Tunnel (3.399 meters) in Makwanpur, under the Kathmandu-Tarai/Madhes Fast Track Road, which is a national pride project constructed under army management, President Paudel mentioned that the Army has been working round the clock on national pride projects, including specialized tunnels and bridge constructions.

"Despite the particularly remote geographical conditions, difficult terrain, and adverse situations, the professionalism, efficiency, and dedication to the nation that the army has long shown in building national roads and infrastructure is commendable and exemplary," the Head-of-the-State said.

President Paudel expressed his belief that the construction of a modern 71-kilometer expressway directly connecting the Kathmandu Valley with the Tarai-Madhes will bring a qualitative change to the country's transportation system.

“This project will significantly reduce travel time and distance, which will also lead to notable savings in fuel consumption and vehicle operation and maintenance costs. I have seen that the Nepal government and the Army are committed to completing the project on time, which will play an important role in the country's economic and social transformation through its significant contribution to the national economy,” he added.

The President expressed the belief that the importance of this project is not limited to just physical infrastructure development, but will also play a significant role in reducing the geographical distance between the capital Kathmandu and the Tarai-Madhesh region, as well as in strengthening social harmony, mutual tolerance, and national unity.

He said, "I expect this project to have far-reaching and significant contributions to promoting tourism, facilitating trade and transport, expanding regional economic activities, and achieving sustainable development goals. I believe that with effective coordination and full commitment to responsibilities during the project construction, the Nepali Army will have everyone's support without leaving any effort behind."

The programme was attended by Bagmati Province Chief Deepak Prasad Devkota, Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal, Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming, South Korean Ambassador Park Jae-kyung, and Army Chief Ashok Raj Sigdel, among other dignitaries. (RSS)
